applied.old: Why don't these drugs work on calcified PTSD? Because even if they did work for mood by modulating serotonin transmission, PTSD is not a mood disorder. That's a bit like putting some Bengay on a broken leg. This protocol tries to get at the underpinnings of the problem. The ketone BHB blocks enzymes called HDACs ([Shimazu, et al, 2013](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/4w889738)), and in mice that couldn't hold on to extinction learning (learning that a cue is now safe), an HDAC blocker made the new learning last ([Whittle & Singewald, 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3961057)). In people with PTSD, the first small study of a keto diet with BHB supplements found that both people who finished its four weeks improved, by 20 and 10 points on the standard 80-point PTSD checklist, which its authors call clinically meaningful ([Edwards, et al, 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39588043/)). In two case reports, women whose PTSD hadn't responded to treatment were nearly or fully free of symptoms after months on the diet ([Bellamy & Laurent, 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40626225/); [Laurent, 2026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41783812/)). No controlled trial of the diet has been done yet, and the one placebo-controlled trial of BHB supplements alone was too small to tell either way ([Youssef, et al, 2022](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36282607/)), although we can see some astounding BHB salt reviews on forums, like for [brain injury repair](https://www.reddit.com/r/keto/comments/1fmu0po/ketone_supplements_insanely_good/), and BHB injections work for rats with trauma, although in humans it's still an open question whether the salts work as well as the keto diet ([Engelhardt, et al, 2026](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1854499/full)).

applied.old: The Fix: If the brain is burning less sugar, we give it another fuel. Ketones are its backup fuel, and brains that take up less glucose (as in early Alzheimer's) still take up ketones normally ([Cunnane, et al, 2016](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/molecular-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnmol.2016.00053/text)). PQQ made mouse cells build more mitochondria, the parts of the cell that burn fuel ([Chowanadisai, et al, 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2804159)); whether it does that in the human brain hasn't been shown.
applied.new: The Fix: If your brain is burning less sugar, give it ketones, which it can consume instead. Ketones work even when the brain isn't able to burn glucose efficiently, as in early Alzheimer's ([Cunnane, et al, 2016](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/molecular-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnmol.2016.00053/text)). And [one man's Alzheimer's improved markedly](https://www.longecity.org/forum/viewtopic.php?t=1025608) on coconut oil, and later on a ketone drink ([Newport, et al, 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25301680/)). We've also got an early Parkinson's study with 5 people (no control group) who improved a lot after a month on a ketogenic diet ([VanItallie, et al, 2005](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728303/)). In a bigger randomized Parkinson's trial, people on keto got more relief from fatigue, thinking difficulty, and daytime sleepiness than those on a low-fat diet. Movement improved about the same on both ([Phillips, et al, 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30098269/)). And as for PQQ, it made mouse cells build more mitochondria, the parts of a cell that burn fuel ([Chowanadisai, et al, 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2804159)), but that hasn't been shown in the human brain.
